title: The Woman Who Taught Six Girls
shortDescription: A child bride of nine who could not read, married in 1840, she qualified as a teacher at sixteen, opened India's first girls' school on New Year's Day 1848 with six pupils — and was pelted with stones and dung on the way. Eighteen schools, a well dug in her own yard, a refuge where widows could bring a baby and leave it, and a pyre she lit herself because others said the last rites were not hers to perform.
heroImageAlt: A painted portrait showing two women seated close together, one of them Savitribai Phule, the other her colleague Fatima Sheikh. It is a later oil painting, not a photograph.
heroImageCaption: Savitribai Phule with Fatima Sheikh. This is not a photograph. It is a painted portrait made around the year 2000 for the Government of Maharashtra, and no photograph of the two women together is known to exist.
introduction: Every schoolchild in India is told the date: 1 January 1848, the day India's first school for girls opened. Six pupils enrolled. Stones, mud and cow dung were thrown at the teacher on the way. She was about seventeen, a child bride who had been married at nine and could not read when the wedding happened. Her name was Savitribai Phule, and over the next nine years she and her husband opened eighteen schools, were thrown out of their house for it, and became the first Indian women to run a school of their own. This is the story that survives — and the parts of it that turned out to belong to somebody else.

chapters.heading: The Village That Would Not Have Her
paragraphs: Begin with a well. In the villages of western India in 1831, the village well was not a public convenience. It was a checkpoint. Families at the bottom of the caste order — the ones called *Mahars* and *Mangs*, who performed work the upper castes considered ritually polluting, from sweeping to carrying night soil — were not allowed to draw water from it. They dug their own wells, at a distance, if they could afford the labour. To be refused water was not an inconvenience. It was the daily, physical announcement that you were not fully human in the eyes of everyone around you.

Caste in nineteenth-century India was a system of inherited rank, and untouchability was its floor. It was enforced less by law than by daily refusals: a shared well, a temple doorway, a rope, a courtyard, a marriage. The law would not abolish it; it mostly described it.

Savitribai was born on 3 January 1831 in Naigaon, a village in Khandala taluka of Satara district in what is now Maharashtra — the Marathi-speaking western part of India, then governed from Bombay by the East India Company, a private British trading firm that would not become a crown colony for another twenty-seven years. Her father, Khandoji Nevse Patil, was the village headman, the *patil*, which meant he collected the land revenue the Company demanded. Her mother was Lakshmibai, and she had three brothers. Note the shape of that household: a family with authority inside the village system, and outside the boundary of its water supply.

You will often read that a small Savitribai was turned away from the village school, and that her father was driven out of the village by the panchayat — the village council — for trying to educate her. It is one of the most repeated sentences about her, and no record supports it. What does survive is her husband's own statement, given in writing in 1852 to a Christian missionary magazine: when he began teaching girls, it did not please his own caste people and his own parents threw him out of the house. The anecdote has been swapped between the two of them over a century and a half. Savitribai's own childhood is, honestly, mostly undocumented — so let us move to the part that is documented, because that part is extraordinary enough.

chapters.heading: A Girl of Nine Who Could Not Read
paragraphs: She was married in 1840, when she was about nine years old. Child marriage was then the ordinary practice, not an extremity, and there is no single national age at which it happened; it was common for a girl to be married before she could read. Savitribai could not read when the wedding took place. Whatever her life had been in Naigaon, it had not included books.

Her husband was Jyotirao Phule, born in 1827 in the village of Katgaon, a *Maval* Brahmin — the upper-caste community that ran the temples, the courts and the schools that she would spend her life challenging. He lost his young parents, was raised by a sister-in-law named Sagunabai Kshirsagar who taught him to read and encouraged him, worked as a clerk, studied, and qualified as a *pleader*, a lawyer who pleads in court. He also held the post of public notary. He was, by the standards of a poor Brahmin family in 1840, doing well.

In his own house he did something no one in it had done: he taught his wife to read and write. She learned quickly, and then she kept going. She trained as a teacher at institutions run by Christian missionaries — one in Ahmednagar, run by an American missionary woman named Cynthia Farrar, and one in Poona, the Normal School. In 1847, at sixteen, she became a qualified teacher. It is generally accepted that she was the first formally trained female teacher in India. That is not a small sentence: the woman who was a nine-year-old illiterate bride four years earlier had, at sixteen, been inside a professional training course that almost no Indian woman of any class had ever attended.

They lived in a *wada* — a family house with rooms around a shared courtyard — in Poona, the city now spelled Pune, about 150 kilometres from where she had been born. It is a modest building in the old part of the city, and it is now a small museum. Hold on to that building. The story turns on it twice.

media.alt: The exterior of the Phule Wada, a courtyard house in Pune that was the home of Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule and is now a small museum.
media.caption: The Phule Wada in Pune. The Phules were turned out of this house in 1849. It is now a museum, and the one photograph everyone knows of Savitribai Phule was made from a group portrait taken here.

chapters.heading: Six Girls, and Stones
paragraphs: On 1 January 1848, Savitribai and Jyotirao opened a school in a room lent to them by a friend, Tatyasaheb Bhide. It was in Bhide's house in Poona, and it is generally accepted as the first school for girls ever founded in India. Six girls were enrolled.

On the first day, a group of men who opposed them shouted obscenities at her and threw cow dung at her. The Maharashtrian state encyclopedia records the phrase they used — *dharmbudila*, accusing her of buggering religion — and records that she did not step back. Later accounts add stones and mud to the dung. The reception is the one thing about this school that nobody argues about: the idea of a girl from a lower caste teaching a girl from a higher one was treated by some of Poona's residents as an attack on religion itself.

She was about seventeen. She was a child bride, a beginner's teacher, and a woman with no legal rights at all — under the law then in force she could not own property, inherit, or be a party to a contract. She also carried a spare sari, because the attacks came on the road. And she did not have long to make the school matter: it closed within about a year.

What she did next is the actual achievement. In 1849 she started a school for adults — for women who had never been allowed to be students at any age. That same year Jyotirao's own father asked them to leave the family house, on the grounds that what they were doing was a sin. A lawyer with a license, a qualified teacher with a certificate, and a curriculum, evicted. They moved in with their friend Usman Sheikh, and there Savitribai worked alongside his sister, Fatima Sheikh, who had trained at the same Normal School and became, in the accounts of her biographer Nasreen Sayyed, the first Muslim woman teacher in India.

They kept going. They established two trusts in the 1850s to fund the work, one for a girls' school in Poona and one for the education of Mahar, Mang and other castes treated as untouchable. They taught children of different castes in the same room, which in 1850 was a declaration. When poor families pulled their daughters out because they needed the wages, Savitribai began paying small stipends so the girls would stay.

And they dug a well. Lower-caste families were forbidden the village water; the Phules dug one in the yard behind their own house, for them. It caused a furor. Consider what that act was: not a speech, not a pamphlet, a hole in the ground, next to their door, that said the rule did not apply here.

The number that survives best is Jyotirao's own. Asked in 1852 what he had done, he answered in a Christian missionary periodical called *Dnyanodaya*: eighteen schools, for girls and for children of different castes. Eighteen is the best-attested figure. How many girls passed through in total is not known, because no official return has been found — and the precise enrolment numbers that circulate online cannot be traced to a document. Use eighteen; leave the rest open.

The British response should stop you. The colonial state that forced the *sati* ban through in 1829, and would pass the widow-remarriage law of 1856 while these two were already working, named her the finest teacher in its largest province. Her pupils were the daughters of families the law did not count. A government that treated untouchability as a reformable abuse but never touched the hierarchy had no category for what she was doing, so it congratulated her instead.

chapters.heading: The Shelter for Widows
paragraphs: Because Savitribai's pupils were mostly from families the new widow-remarriage law of 1856 did not reach, her problem was not only schooling. It was what happened to a girl before she was old enough to be a pupil, and what happened to a woman after her husband died.

In 1854 she opened a shelter for widows in Poona. The need was specific and horrifying. A widow who was young and had no son, or no family to take her back, was liable under the system to be pressured or paid to kill herself — *sati*, the immolation of a widow on her husband's funeral pyre. The British had abolished sati in 1829, twenty-five years earlier, and banned it with a capital punishment attached. It went on anyway, because it ran on family consent, custom, and the fact that a poor woman's death solved a neighbour's problem. Very often, too, a widow's newborn child went with her, because a baby with no father and no caste was nobody's responsibility.

So the shelter offered something very modern: a place to bring a baby, and a choice. A pamphlet advertised it roughly this way — widows, come here and deliver your baby safely and secretly, and decide whether to keep the child or leave it, and we will take care of it. In 1864 they enlarged the work to take in destitute women and child brides cast off by their families, and educated them. It ran for years.

In 1874 the couple took in a boy whose mother had come to that shelter to give birth to him. He was the son of a Brahmin widow, and he grew up to become a doctor. Savitribai and Jyotirao had no children of their own. In a society organised entirely around who inherits and who is a legitimate heir, a man who adopts a child of a different caste from a shelter for abandoned babies has already made several statements without making any.

And in 1873 Jyotirao founded the Satyashodhak Samaj, the Society of Truth Seekers, a group that met to break caste practice from below. Its most concrete invention was the wedding it invented. A Satyashodhak marriage had no Brahmin priest to officiate, because the priest's fee and authority were part of the machine, and no dowry. The couple took an oath instead, pledging themselves to education and equality. Savitribai is credited with starting that practice. It is worth pausing on what a wedding without a priest meant in 1870s India: it removed the one professional whose presence at a marriage made it socially legitimate, and replaced him with a promise made by the two people getting married.

Savitribai is often read as an appendix to her husband. The political scientist Bidyut Chakrabarty argues she was the one nineteenth-century female reformer in India who consciously held caste and gender together as a single problem. Dhananjay Keer, Jyotirao's biographer, wrote that there is hardly any parallel in the nineteenth century to a life devoted like hers to the uplift of the Indian woman — and regretted how little of it had been recognised. Her work is most often filed under someone else's name.

chapters.heading: Go, Get Education
paragraphs: Around the middle of the nineteenth century, a woman who wanted to change something in India had three tools: a pamphlet, a speech, or a school. Savitribai used all three, and she also wrote poetry, which in a country with almost no publishing for women of any class was an act of defiance rather than a literary choice.

Her collection *Kavya Phule* appeared in 1854. Its most reproduced poem is known in English translation as "Go, Get Education". The translation published in Braj Ranjan Mani's scholarly edition of her writings gives its argument plainly: "Sit idle no more, go, get education / End misery of the oppressed and forsaken." Elsewhere in the same work she tells the oppressed to throw away the Brahmin's scriptures. Not all of India was governed by Brahmin texts, but those texts were what the courts, the temples and the schools ran on, and she was telling the people they had been taught to regard as lowest to stop asking permission from them.

The instruction is delivered as an instruction. It is not a plea. Read the imperative of it — go, get, throw away, end — and you have her whole method: she did not spend her career petitioning the powerful for permission. She built the thing, and told people to use it.

Her second collection, *Bavan Kashi Subodh Ratnakar*, appeared in 1891 and contains fifty-two short poems. The number is the reason for the title, and the number is a date: her husband had died the previous year, and there is a poem for each week of that year. Fifty-two quatrains in a handwritten manuscript, in her own hand. A poem for every week of her first year alone: a woman processing something she had no one else to say it to. In a published translation of her poetry, the term used for the oppressed is the word Dalit uses today, more than a century early.

Which brings up her face. The image of Savitribai Phule that everyone knows — two women seated together, one in a blue sari — is not a photograph, and not contemporary. No photograph of her and Fatima Sheikh together is known. The only two official portraits that exist are oil paintings made around the year 2000 for the Government of Maharashtra, by an art teacher in Pune, Vilas Chormala, and by Suhir Katkar of the J.J. School of Art in Mumbai, painted from the only known photographic basis for her face: a group photograph in which Jyotirao is seated. A researcher on the state's own Phule publication committee has stated that apart from the two photographs issued with that set, the circulating images of her are fanciful, and the standard academic history of the movement says the same. A 2026 fact-check caught a photograph shared widely as Savitribai that is in fact Janakibai Banker, mother of Shantabai Banker, who wrote the first biography of Savitribai Phule in 1939 and was for decades forgotten herself. A person does not get erased by being hated; she gets erased by being replaced with a version that is easier to circulate.

media.alt: A room inside the museum in the Phule Wada, Pune, with display cases holding documents and objects.
media.caption: Inside the museum in the Phule Wada. Savitribai's handwritten manuscripts, including the fifty-two quatrains of Bavan Kashi Subodh Ratnakar, are kept in collections like this one.

chapters.heading: She Lit the Pyre
paragraphs: On 28 November 1890, Jyotirao Phule died. He had been a schoolboy who became a lawyer, a notary, a writer, an anti-caste organiser, and a man whose title *Mahatma* — great soul — had been applied to him publicly. He was sixty-three.

His funeral became a dispute, and the dispute became the most quoted scene in the movement. Relatives blocked the rites on the ground that they could not be performed by the couple's adopted son, Yashwant, because of his birth circumstances. The Maharashtrian state encyclopedia records that Savitribai did not argue: she set fire to her husband's body herself. The last rites were men's work, and a woman performing them at a public funeral was a breach with an almost physical charge to it. She was fifty-nine. In 1893 she chaired the Satyashodhak Conference at Saswad, south of Pune.

Then the last seven years. In 1897 bubonic plague arrived in the area south of Poona — the third plague pandemic, a disease carried by the fleas of rats. Savitribai and Yashwant opened a clinic for plague patients on the southern outskirts, in a spot chosen because it was clear of the infection. She was sixty-six, and she was a teacher by training, not a doctor. When she learned that the son of Pandurang Babaji Gaekwad, from the Mahar settlement outside Mundhwa, had caught the plague, she personally walked him to hospital — and caught the disease herself doing it. She died on 10 March 1897. Some accounts of the state's own commemorations give 19 March. A woman who nursed plague patients until she was told to take a sick boy to hospital is a woman who did not consider being a teacher a limit on what she was for.

Hold that ending against the beginning: a nine-year-old bride who could not read, turned out of her father-in-law's house for teaching girls, presiding over a conference, and then carrying a patient to hospital as the plague took her. The through-line is not money, or status, or even a movement. It is that she kept taking responsibility for whoever was in front of her, and never once asked whether she was the sort of person allowed to. We have very nearly lost her, and what we have kept is mostly a set of pictures somebody imagined.

One honest footnote. It is often said that Savitribai was refused cremation when she died, and buried without a marker in an outcaste burial ground, and that a symbolic grave was later built for her. Researchers have looked. The state encyclopedia, Britannica, the standard academic study, and her first biographer's 1939 account do not describe her funeral at all. There is no register entry, because the municipal staff were not available to record the death. Say that, rather than repeat the burial story, which may well be true and cannot be shown.

media.alt: A stone statue outdoors showing Jyotirao Phule seated and Savitribai Phule standing beside him.
media.caption: A statue of the Phules at Badvel in Andhra Pradesh. Statues of the pair are now common across India — the highest-volume record of her life is not a photograph or a schoolbook but a line of stone figures in public squares.

chapters.heading: The Long After
paragraphs: Savitribai died in 1897. The Government of India, which had applauded her in 1852, did not issue a stamp for her until 1998 — a hundred years after her death, on the centenary, Rs 2, twenty-four million of them.

What came after was slow, then suddenly fast. From 1995 her birthday on 3 January has been observed in Maharashtra as *Balika Din*, Girl Child Day — the most direct possible honour for a woman who opened the first girls' school in India on that date. In 2014 the state legislature renamed the University of Poona for her. On 14 February 2022 a full-length statue of her was unveiled on that campus. In 2019 a Hindi film about the pair, *Phule*, directed by Pratik Gandhi, was released on National Girl Child Day.

In May 2026, botanists publishing in the peer-reviewed journal *Phytotaxa* named a new flowering plant after her, *Crotalaria phulei*, from the Nagpur district: a small shrub with bright yellow flowers, its conservation status recorded as data deficient because they did not yet know enough about it. Naming a species is the most durable thing that can happen to a person, because a species cannot be argued with.

In April 2025, the Maharashtra government approved ₹142.60 crore for a memorial at Naigaon, ten acres at her birthplace, including a women's training centre. In the village where she was born there was, until recently, no sign that she had existed.

That is the record. One stamp, one university, one statue, one film, one plant, one funding approval — against a woman who ran eighteen schools, dug a well, sheltered widows, invented a wedding, and then set fire to her husband's body in front of a crowd. And the picture of her is a painting made in the year 2000, from a group photograph in which her husband is the only person in focus.

The line to keep is hers. Sit idle no more, go, get education; end misery of the oppressed and forsaken. It is an instruction, in the imperative, written in 1854 by a sixteen-year-old who had been a bride at nine, to people like her. It is not a plea for permission. It is a thing to be done, and it was the method of her entire life — she taught the six girls first, and then went and got the world.

media.alt: A commemorative Indian postage stamp issued in 1998 showing Savitribai Phule, printed in brown and black.
media.caption: The India Post stamp of 10 March 1998, issued on the centenary of her death, one hundred years after the Government of India had called her the best teacher in the Bombay Presidency.

challenge: A child bride of nine, married in 1840, who could not read and had no legal rights of any kind, was refused entry to most institutions, pelted with stones and cow dung for teaching six girls, and evicted from her father-in-law's house for it.
journey: Trained as a teacher in 1847 at sixteen, opened the first girls' school in India on 1 January 1848 with six pupils, and over the next five years built eighteen schools, two trusts, a well for people forbidden the village water, a shelter where widows could safely bring a newborn, and a form of wedding with no priest and no dowry — while writing poetry that told the oppressed to get an education and throw away the Brahmin's scriptures.
achievement: Widely regarded as India's first formally trained female teacher and the founder of its first school for girls; in 1852 the British administration named her the best teacher in the Bombay Presidency.
impact: Her methods — mixed-caste classrooms, stipends to keep poor girls enrolled, manual and industrial training for women, and the poet's argument that education was the lever on both caste and gender — are taught today as the founding curriculum of women's education and of Dalit feminism in India.
lesson: She never asked whether she was the sort of person allowed to do any of it. Teach the six girls first, and then go and get the world.
